settings.heading: Good intentions, different timelines
settings.text:
Whether an idea comes from the left or the right, it often begins with a belief that people should be able to live meaningful, secure, flourishing lives. Most people are not trying to make the world worse. They are disagreeing about how to improve it—and about when the improvement should arrive.

One political instinct looks toward the long term. It wants to build the technology, infrastructure, institutions, and wealth that might make a better future possible. It is willing to accept sacrifice now in the name of what could exist later.

Another political instinct looks at the present. It asks who is suffering now, who is being asked to wait, and who is being sacrificed for someone else's vision of tomorrow. It is suspicious of futures that require people living today to endure indefinitely.

Both instincts contain something important. A society that only manages the present may never build the capacity to change. A society that sacrifices the present for a distant future can lose sight of the people it claims to be serving.

settings.heading: The future cannot come at this cost
settings.text:
The future is not a moral blank cheque.

We can only ask people to sacrifice so much of their time, security, health, freedom, and dignity for a promise that may arrive decades from now. Progress that requires abandoning the living is not automatically progress.

We need to build for tomorrow without treating today as disposable. That means improving the conditions people live in now while developing the tools, institutions, and communities that make a better future possible.

The question is not whether we should care about the future or the present. The question is why we keep treating them as enemies.

settings.heading: Progress with a human timeline
settings.text:
World in Common is interested in projects that do both:

  • reduce suffering now
  • build long-term capacity
  • create useful infrastructure that people can access today
  • protect the future without making the present unbearable
  • measure progress by human flourishing, not only by growth or technical achievement

A better system should not require us to choose between hope and immediate care.
Build the future without abandoning the present.

settings.heading: Open Source Is a Commons
settings.text:
Open-source software is more than a technical method. It is a way of contributing to a shared public infrastructure.

When someone releases useful software openly, other people can inspect it, learn from it, improve it, adapt it, and build on top of it. The value does not remain locked inside one company. It becomes part of a commons.

That is a form of rebellion against the idea that every useful tool must be owned, rented, and controlled by a giant platform.

settings.heading: AI changes the equation
settings.text:
AI makes software development faster and more accessible. That creates a danger: people may use AI to produce more closed tools for more powerful companies, making the same concentrated system even stronger.

But the same tools can also be used in the opposite direction. People can use AI to build, document, test, translate, and maintain open-source alternatives—and then release the source, the documentation, and the improvements back to everyone.

The important question is not simply whether AI wrote the code. The question is: who can inspect it, use it, improve it, and own the infrastructure built around it?

AI-generated code should still be reviewed by humans, tested, documented, and released under a clear licence. Open source is not automatically good, secure, or sustainable. It becomes a public contribution when people take responsibility for maintaining it.

settings.heading: From consumers to contributors
settings.text:
A closed tool turns us into users. An open tool can turn us into participants.

We do not need to recreate every platform from scratch. Many of the tools controlled by large companies are no longer technically mysterious. The difficult part is often maintenance, trust, distribution, governance, and sustainable funding—not magic.

Open source gives us a way to redirect value:

  • from rented access to shared infrastructure
  • from passive consumption to contribution
  • from platform dependence to interoperability
  • from proprietary black boxes to inspectable tools
  • from a few owners extracting value to many people building capacity together

This is not a promise that every open-source project will replace a giant company. It is a commitment to build more of the tools we want to depend on.

settings.heading: Open source as social contribution
settings.text:
Software is infrastructure. It shapes how we communicate, work, learn, organize, and exchange value.

Contributing code, documentation, translations, design, testing, support, or funding is a way of improving the environment other people live in.

You do not need to start a company to make a contribution. You can fix a bug, write documentation, answer a question, report a vulnerability, translate an interface, or help maintain a project that thousands of people rely on.

The commons is built by people who decide that useful things should not disappear behind a login screen.

settings.heading: What we are trying to do
settings.text:
World in Common will use AI where it helps us move faster—but we will try to direct the output toward shared tools, open knowledge, and public alternatives.

We will be transparent about what is AI-assisted. We will not pretend that AI removes the need for human judgement, maintenance, or accountability.

The goal is simple:
Use the machines to build tools that make people less dependent on the machines' owners.

settings.heading: Transparency note
settings.text: If we publish software or code created with AI assistance, we should identify the level of assistance and publish the relevant licence, repository, documentation, and known limitations. The point is not to claim purity. The point is to make the contribution inspectable and useful to other people.

settings.title: Technofeudalism
settings.author: Yanis Varoufakis
settings.note: Argues that cloud platforms have replaced markets with something closer to fiefdoms. It also remembers that the first internet ran on common, open protocols that anyone could use for free.

settings.title: The Man Who Quit Money
settings.author: Mark Sundeen
settings.note: Daniel Suelo stopped using money. The book asks how much of our relationship with money is necessary—and how much we have simply accepted by default.

settings.title: Broken Money
settings.author: Lyn Alden
settings.note: A history of money as a ledger, and of why the financial system fails so many of the people who depend on it.

settings.title: The Price of Tomorrow
settings.author: Jeff Booth
settings.note: Technology keeps making things cheaper. An economy built on ever-growing credit has to fight that.

settings.title: Sapiens
settings.author: Yuval Noah Harari
settings.note: How shared stories—money among them—let millions of strangers cooperate.

settings.title: Island
settings.author: Aldous Huxley
settings.note: Huxley’s last novel imagines a small society organised around human flourishing, and asks what it would take to protect it.

settings.name: Yanis Varoufakis
settings.note: Economist and former Greek finance minister. Author of Technofeudalism.

settings.name: Jonathan Haidt
settings.note: Social psychologist. Writes about how social media changes childhood and public life.

settings.name: Daniel Suelo
settings.note: Lived for years without money. The subject of The Man Who Quit Money.

settings.name: Judy Heumann
settings.note: Disability rights activist who fought for access as a civil right.

settings.heading: Influences
settings.intro: The books and people that formed our views. We do not agree with everything any of them says.
